intro: Four modules take you from your first commit to a confident team workflow: how Git tracks work, branching and merging, remotes and pull requests, and safe ways to undo mistakes. Practice in the labs and keep the Reference tab open as a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Version control and the Git workflow
modules.summary: Understand what Git tracks and the three places your work lives, then make your first repository, commits and history.

blocks.p: Git records snapshots of a project over time. Every snapshot (a commit) has an author, a message and a unique ID, so you can see what changed, why, and go back. It works offline: your computer holds the whole history in a repository.

list: Undo a mistake without losing other work
Work on a feature without breaking the main code
See who changed a line and why (git blame, git log)

guide.h: Working tree, staging area and repository

blocks.p: Changes move through three places. You edit files in the working tree, choose what goes into the next commit by adding it to the staging area (also called the index), and commit to save the staged snapshot in the repository.

steps.d: Change files in your folder (working tree).
git add file picks the changes for the next commit.

cmds: Start a new repository in the current folder
Copy an existing repository, with its history
What is changed, staged or untracked
Stage a file (git add . stages everything here)
Short history, one line per commit
head: Command
What it does

blocks.note: Set your identity once: git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email you@example.com. Every commit records it.

tips: Run git status often. It tells you what state you are in and what to do next.
Write commit messages that say why, in the imperative: "Fix login timeout", not "stuff".
Commit small, related changes. Small commits are easy to review and to undo.
terms: The folder's tracked files plus their full history, stored in a hidden .git folder.
A saved snapshot with an ID, author, date and message.
The files you see and edit on disk.
Where you collect the changes that will go into the next commit.
A pointer to the commit you currently have checked out.
The unique ID of a commit, such as a1b2c3d.

slides.title: Git in one picture
bullets: Three places: working tree, staging area, repository
History is a chain of snapshots
script: Git tracks snapshots of your project. Your changes flow from the working tree, to the staging area, to the repository.

slides.title: Your first repository
script: Start with git init in a folder, or clone an existing project. Then add and commit your changes.

visual.text:
git init
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add readme"
git status

slides.title: Reading history
script: Git log lists commits newest first. Use the oneline option when you only need a quick overview.

visual.text:
git log --oneline
 a1b2c3d Fix login timeout
 9f8e7d6 Add readme

slides.title: Good commits
script: Small, focused commits with clear messages make history useful. Never commit secrets such as passwords or access keys.

modules.title: Branching and merging
modules.summary: Use branches to work in parallel, then bring the work back together and resolve conflicts.

blocks.p: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. Creating one is instant and cheap, so you can try an idea on its own line of work without touching the main code. The default branch is usually called main.

cmds: List branches (the current one is starred)
Create a branch and move to it
head: Command
What it does

blocks.p: git merge feature-x brings that branch's commits into the one you are on. If main has not moved, Git simply slides the pointer forward (a fast-forward). If both have new commits, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

head: Situation
Result
rows: Both sides changed the same lines

blocks.p: A conflict means Git cannot decide between two edits. It marks the file with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines.

steps.d: Find the markers and choose or combine the right text.
The file must be exactly what you want.

blocks.note: To back out of a merge you do not want: git merge --abort.

tips: Make a new branch for every task. Keep main working.
Pull the latest main into your branch regularly so conflicts stay small.
Read the conflict markers carefully. Never just keep one side without looking.
terms: A lightweight pointer to a commit, used for parallel lines of work.
Combine another branch's history into the current branch.
A merge where Git only moves the pointer because there is nothing to combine.
Two changes to the same lines that Git cannot combine automatically.
Replay your commits on top of another branch for a linear history.
A short-lived branch for one task or fix.

slides.title: Branches are pointers
script: A branch is only a pointer to a commit, so creating one is instant. Keep main stable and do your work on a feature branch.

slides.title: Create, switch, merge
script: Create a branch, commit on it, switch back to main and merge it in.

visual.text:
git switch -c feature-login
# edit, add, commit
git switch main
git merge feature-login
git branch -d feature-login

slides.title: Fast-forward or merge commit
bullets: No new work on main: fast-forward
script: Git picks the simplest outcome. Only when both sides edit the same lines does it need your decision.

slides.title: Fixing a conflict
script: Open the file, choose the right text, delete the marker lines, stage the file and commit. Use merge abort if you want to start over.

modules.title: Remotes and collaboration
modules.summary: Share work through a remote such as GitHub: fetch, pull, push and review changes with pull requests.

blocks.p: A remote is another copy of the repository, usually on a server such as GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps. The default remote created by git clone is called origin. Your local branches and the remote's branches are separate until you sync them.

cmds: Download new commits without changing your files
Fetch, then merge into your current branch
Upload your commits to the remote
Push a new branch and remember it
head: Command
What it does

steps.d: Commit small changes on your branch.
Open a pull request so teammates can review.
After approval, merge and delete the branch.

blocks.p: A rejected push ("non-fast-forward") means the remote has commits you do not. Run git pull (or git fetch then merge or rebase), resolve any conflicts, then push again.

blocks.note: Avoid git push --force on shared branches: it can erase teammates' work. If you must, use --force-with-lease.
Add a .gitignore file so build output, logs and secret files such as .env are never committed.

tips: git fetch is always safe. It only downloads; git pull also changes your branch.
Never push passwords or tokens. If you do, treat them as leaked and rotate them.
Keep pull requests small and describe what and why.
terms: A copy of the repository hosted elsewhere.
The default name for the remote you cloned from.
Download new data from a remote without merging.
Fetch and merge in one step.
Send your local commits to a remote branch.
A request to merge a branch, with review and discussion.

slides.title: Local and remote
bullets: Sync with fetch, pull and push
script: Your repository and the remote are separate copies. You sync them with fetch, pull and push.

slides.title: Pull versus fetch
script: Fetch downloads new commits and leaves your files alone. Pull also merges them into your branch.

slides.title: Branch, push, pull request
script: Work on a branch, push it, and open a pull request. A teammate reviews before it is merged.

visual.text:
git switch -c fix-typo
git commit -am "Fix typo"
git push -u origin fix-typo

slides.title: Safe sharing
script: Ignore files that should never be shared and never commit credentials. Avoid force pushing on shared branches.

modules.title: Undoing mistakes and recovering work
modules.summary: Choose the right undo for the situation: restore files, amend, revert, reset, stash and reflog.

head: Situation
Command
rows: Discard edits to a file (not staged)
Unstage a file, keep the edits
Fix the last commit's message or contents
Set work aside for a moment

blocks.note: git reset --hard can destroy uncommitted work. Check git status first. Do not reset commits that others already pulled; use git revert instead.

blocks.p: Git remembers where HEAD has been. git reflog lists those moves, including commits that are no longer on any branch. Find the hash and run git switch -c rescue <hash> to get it back. Reflog entries are local and expire after a few weeks.

blocks.note: If a secret was committed, removing it in a new commit is not enough: it stays in history. Rotate the secret, then clean history with an approved tool (for example git filter-repo) and coordinate with your team.

tips: Rule of thumb: rewrite history only on commits nobody else has. Otherwise revert.
git stash is great when you must switch branches in the middle of work.
Before anything risky, create a backup branch: git branch backup.
terms: Discard or unstage changes to files.
Create a new commit that undoes an earlier one, without rewriting history.
Move the current branch (and optionally the index and files) to another commit.
Replace the last commit with an updated one.
A local log of where HEAD has pointed, used to recover commits.

slides.title: Undo toolbox
script: Different mistakes need different tools. Start by asking whether the commit is already shared.

slides.title: Reset, carefully
script: Reset moves your branch back. The hard mode also overwrites your working files, so use it with care.

slides.title: Revert a bad commit
script: Revert creates a new commit that reverses the old one. It is the safe choice when others already have the commit.

visual.text:
git log --oneline
git revert a1b2c3d
git push

slides.title: Find lost work
bullets: Create a branch at the hash
script: Reflog helps you find commits that seem lost. If you ever commit a secret, rotate it right away.
